candidate.answerReason: The watch advances at 24/25 of the actual rate. Advancing 600 displayed minutes takes 625 actual minutes after noon, reaching 10:25 PM.

methods.label: Compare watch time with actual time
methods.explanation:
Measure both elapsed times from noon, when the watch was correct. In \(60\) actual minutes, the watch advances
\[
57+\frac{36}{60}=57.6\text{ minutes}.
\]
Because its rate is constant, the ratio of displayed elapsed time to actual elapsed time is always
\[
\frac{57.6}{60}=\frac{24}{25}.
\]
From noon to a displayed \(10{:}00\) PM is \(10\) hours, or \(600\) displayed minutes. If \(t\) is the actual number of minutes since noon, then
\[
\frac{24}{25}t=600,
\qquad
 t=600\cdot\frac{25}{24}=625.
\]
This is \(10\) hours and \(25\) minutes after noon. The watch advances steadily at a positive rate, so this is the first time it reaches that reading. The actual time is \(10{:}25\) PM, choice C.
methods.levelReason: Time-unit conversion and direct proportionality solve the clock problem without advanced rate models.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task asks for an unknown actual duration from a fixed relationship between actual and displayed elapsed times. The method establishes direct proportionality and solves for that duration. Time conversion, elapsed-time interpretation, and fraction division support the route; inverse proportionality is not used.
